source.title: How Many Parameters Does it Take to Change a Light Bulb? Evaluating Performance in Self-Play of Conversational Games as a Function of Model Characteristics
source.authors: Nidhir Bhavsar; Jonathan Jordan; Sherzod Hakimov; D. Schlangen

record.tranche_reason: The study measures performance on an interactive downstream benchmark across models of different sizes, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or running controlled scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports clembench performance against model size and training-data size, and separately reports scores for same-base-model derivatives, inference backends, and quantization settings. It does not measure cross-entropy loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or investigate compute-optimal allocation. Cited scaling-law findings are not study results.
record.test_reason: Regresses clembench interactive-game scores on log parameter count and training-data size across about 20 existing models. This is a direct result on V6 (downstream scaling) in a new agentive self-play setting. It has no loss measurements or controlled training runs.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Scale (parameters and training-data amount) accounts for a large portion of clembench performance. Instruction-tuning data mix and method also strongly matter. The inference implementation has a notable influence, while milder (8-bit) quantization has little impact.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a cross-sectional clembench comparison across existing models and reports interactive task scores, rather than controlled training runs, held-out loss measurements, or power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that scores vary with inference backend and quantization; it also describes differences among same-base-model instruction-tuned derivatives. It notes possible backend-related differences in input formatting and sampling settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The same model weights score differently across inference backends, by up to about 5 clemscore points for Llama-3-70B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark scores depend on inference backend and unexposed sampling settings.

fits_no_version.finding: 8-bit quantization has negligible impact. 4-bit quantization hurts smaller models more (8B: 19.99 to 11.75; 70B: 35.11 to 33.57).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The performance cost of weight quantization shrinks with model size.

record.problems: The measured benchmark uses English game instances and artificial self-play interactions. Training-data and inference details are unavailable for some models, and backend comparisons may differ in unexposed sampling or formatting settings. The study does not measure loss or conduct controlled scaling runs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows needed for the reported regression, highlighted same-base-model comparison, backend comparison, or quantization comparison. Other individual-model scores and game-level breakdowns in Appendix Tables 4 and 7 and Figures 4–6 were not extracted because they do not add a separate test of scale-versus-downstream-score predictability beyond the aggregate regression and same-base comparisons.

untested.parts: All of it: no pretraining loss is measured and no power-law fit is made.
All of it: there is no extrapolation from small runs.
All of it: compute-optimal allocation is not studied.
All of it: there is no controlled comparison of shape at fixed parameter count.
All of it: there are no other modalities, and no fine-tuning scaling law is measured.
Predictability from pretraining loss, any fitted functional form, and prediction for held-out models.
All of it: no exponents or fitting choices are examined.

missing.what: Per-game scaling dynamics. Taboo improves steadily with size. Wordle improves only for very large models. Imagegame ability seems tied to special training data, not size. Authors see no sudden emergence at any size.
Spread of clemscore within model-size bins across all models, beyond the two same-base families.
Additional same-base families (gemma-7b derivatives 1.82–15.30; mixtral-8x7b derivatives 8.17–15.10) showing within-size spread.

record.verdict_notes: Cross-sectional study of existing models. Some sizes and data amounts are estimated. p-values are reported as 'p < 0.000'. The record's tranche T2 is changed to T3 because this is a new downstream setting (interactive self-play), not a different method on loss. The quantization rows' baselines confound backend: unquantized models ran via HF transformers, quantized ones via llama.cpp.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law relationships in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of power laws fitted on small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their scaling with compute.
Controlled comparisons of architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer as tests of the same power-law form.
The study tests clembench self-play performance, not a range of downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, and the effects of fitting choices or curve bending.

relationships.condition: Aggregate clembench score across about 20 models, regressed on log parameter count (plus training-data size)
relationships.reason: Significant log-linear relation with size (R2 = .57), rising to .67 with training-data size added (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: The significant log-linear size relationship had R² = 0.57, increasing to 0.67 when training-data size was included.

relationships.condition: Instruction-tuned derivatives sharing the same base model and size (mistral-7b, llama-2-70b)
relationships.reason: At fixed size, scores span 6.56–23.64 (7B) and 0.81–21.50 (70B). Fine-tuning data and method, not scale, drive much of the variance (r3–r11).
relationships.display_finding: Scores spanned 6.56–23.64 at 7B and 0.81–21.50 at 70B, with fine-tuning data and method driving much of the variation.
